title: GPU capacity fallbacks and driver/AMI upgrade module for Private VPC
creator: Arielle Chen
description: Deliver a Terraform module and CI-driven workflow that provisions GPU node groups for Redwood Private (VPC) with robust autoscaling fallbacks between ASG and Karpenter, automated AMI/driver upgrades, and production-grade health checks. The module must support mixed instance types (A100/H100), spot vs on-demand fallbacks, instance lifecycle hooks for graceful draining, and be compatible with our private control plane networking and KMS key usage. This ticket covers module design, backward-compatible inputs, tests (terratest + integration), and an upgrade plan for NVIDIA drivers and CUDA across node pools.
acceptance_criteria: Terraform module publishes inputs/outputs and can create both ASG-backed and Karpenter provisioner-backed GPU pools in a customer VPC using existing RBAC and networking

Autoscaling policy supports policy-level fallbacks: prefer spot, fallback to reserved on capacity failure, and route requests to alternative model variants via Smart Routing config in runtime (integration test stub)
Instance lifecycle hooks invoke a drain lambda or kube-controller to ensure KV cache eviction and graceful UI/session handoff; healthcheck endpoint returns 200 within configured TTL post-drain start
CI pipeline validates AMI + NVIDIA driver bundles by booting a test node, running a simple CUDA/GPU inference workload, and passing perf/latency smoke checks
Upgrade playbook (documented in Confluence) provides zero-downtime rolling strategy with canaries and automatic rollback on health regression metrics
implementation_notes: Key design choices: use separate modules for asg and karpenter entrypoints but share common submodules for launch templates, AMI lookup, GPU-driver bootstrap scripts, and lifecycle hooks. Node labels and taints will distinguish dedicated GPU pools (redwood.gpu=true, redwood.pool=dedicated). We'll bake AMIs in Packer with NVIDIA driver versions pinned, and expose an input 'ami_version' to allow safe rollbacks. For spot instances we use mixed_instances_policy on ASG and Karpenter's nodeSelector + provisioner priorities. Health checks include kubelet readiness probe augmentation and an HTTP /healthz/drain-status endpoint served by a small agent (open-source sidecar) that reports KV cache flush status. We will implement an optional 'enable_mig' flag that toggles MIG configuration for A100; initial run will default to false to reduce complexity.
decisions: Favor explicit AMI pinning over dynamic latest-of-family to avoid unexpected kernel/driver mismatches
Expose both ASG and Karpenter flavours. Default to ASG for GA in regulated customers; enable Karpenter opt-in for experimental/dynamic scaling use cases
Implement lifecycle hooks using a Lambda that signals ASG after successful drain to avoid cold-starting model runtimes during drain
MIG support will be experimental behind a flag; full MIG lifecycle (partitioning, device plugin config) deferred to follow-up ticket
tradeoffs: Pinning AMIs increases operational overhead for manual bumps but reduces risk of silent driver regressions — acceptable for Private deployments with strict SLAs
Supporting both ASG and Karpenter increases code surface area; chosen to ensure customers with constrained infra can use ASG while others get elastic autoscaling benefits
Agent sidecar for drain health adds a small memory/CPU overhead on nodes but gives deterministic KV cache flush visibility for rollouts
testing_plan: Unit tests for Terraform modules (tflint + validate), Terratest integration that boots a smallest GPU instance in our shared dev VPC, runs an NVIDIA sanity smoke test (nvidia-smi + simple PyTorch CUDA allocation + tiny inference), and asserts readiness endpoints. Add a simulated spot-interruption test that forces capacity loss and validates fallback to on-demand and Karpenter provisioning. Add GitHub Actions job to run packer job and validate built AMI via a lightweight runner.
rollout_plan: 1) Merge module to infra registry under feature flag; 2) Deploy to internal dev account and run full CI; 3) Canary deploy one private customer cluster with limited model traffic (runtime routing to canary model) and monitor cost/latency/cached hit-rate for 48 hours; 4) Gradual rollout across clusters with automatic rollback on SLO breaches; 5) Post-rollout postmortem and cleanup of old AMIs
